title: Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents
gist: Netflix's Commerce team, presenting at QCon San Francisco 2026, retrofitted its SDLC for AI coding agents mainly through documentation, consistency and review rather than agent-specific work: 45 agent-readable ADRs, AGENTS.md as a robots.txt analogue, a review agent posting only verified blockers, and per-domain GraphRAG served via one MCP tool. The team reported 32% more PRs year over year, no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service, and developer NPS rising from -3 to +25.

themes.theme: Codebases built for humans slow agents

insights.claim: Netflix engineer Mark Khuzam argues that retrofitting the SDLC for AI coding agents was mostly not about agents at all but about documentation, consistency and review.

insights.so_what: AI coding productivity gains depend on organizational engineering hygiene, not just tool purchases.

insights.claim: Netflix's Commerce team found that rolling out Claude Code to every engineer collided with systems built over 20 years for human developers, limiting the promised speed gains.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI coding ROI is gated by legacy codebase readiness, lengthening the adoption curve.
insights.quote: Agents promised speed. But we spent 20 years building for humans.
insights.locator: Khuzam opened with a mock company

insights.claim: Netflix's first attempt to have an AI agent migrate tests took four tries, because internal docs were hard to find before the context window ran out and tests were written inconsistently across the codebase.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Context-window limits and inconsistent code are concrete friction points for agent adoption.

insights.claim: Netflix's Commerce team wrote 45 architecture decision records written for both people and agents, each covering context, decision, pattern, anti-pattern and AI usage notes, and they now ship inside almost every repository.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Agent-readable documentation is becoming a standard engineering investment.
insights.quote: getting what engineers know into what agents see
insights.locator: Khuzam described the fix as context engineering

insights.claim: To keep 45 ADRs and more than 300 other documents findable for agents, Netflix borrowed from search engines, using an AGENTS.md file in the role of robots.txt.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: AGENTS.md is emerging as a de facto standard for agent-facing project instructions.
insights.locator: To keep those records and more

insights.claim: For cross-service work, Netflix found that loading every repository did not fit, Git submodules were brittle, a Git MCP server sees one file rather than the system, and shared copies went stale.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Naive context approaches fail at enterprise scale, creating room for code-knowledge-graph tooling.
insights.quote: sees one file, not the system

insights.claim: Netflix settled on per-domain GraphRAG combining code structure with doc and ADR meaning, pinned to specific commits and served through a single Model Context Protocol tool that Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, a Slack bot and CI review all query, with every answer citing file and line.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: A shared, tool-agnostic context layer reduces lock-in to any single AI coding vendor.
insights.locator: The team needed context that was

insights.claim: At Netflix the CI pipeline remains deterministic, with builds, tests, screenshot diffing, merge queues and canaries, while agents plug into each phase rather than replacing it.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Deterministic CI/CD tooling stays essential alongside AI agents.
insights.locator: The second half of the talk

insights.claim: Netflix's first review agent left 23 comments on a single PR starting with praise; it now posts only verified blockers, each with evidence, a fix and the ADR rule broken.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: AI code review value depends on signal-to-noise; noisy reviewers get ignored.

insights.claim: At Netflix, engineers can add a revise label for an agent to read a review and push a fix, but changes are not yet auto-merged and engineers own the code.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Human ownership remains the governance model even at advanced AI adopters.
insights.quote: Changes aren't yet auto-merged, and engineers own the code.

insights.claim: Netflix's Commerce team reported no Sev 1 incidents in 2026 on a core service and 32% more pull requests year over year after retrofitting its SDLC for AI agents.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Evidence that AI coding agents can raise throughput without degrading reliability when paired with strong process.

insights.claim: Developer Net Promoter Score for Netflix Commerce's internal framework rose from -3 to +25 over three quarters.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Agent-readiness work also improves human developer experience.

insights.claim: Khuzam framed the stakes as shipping agent-written code to Tier 0 services serving more than 300M members without failures.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Large consumer platforms are already putting agent-written code into their most critical services.
insights.quote: what gives us the confidence to ship Tier 0 services to 300M+ members without everything falling apart?
insights.locator: Ahead of the session, Khuzam framed

insights.claim: Khuzam's closing rules are to decide what agents should do and tell them, make it easy to find how to do it, and remember that human judgement still matters, arguing this is simply good engineering for a new reader.
insights.speaker: Andrew Hoblitzell
insights.so_what: Firms with strong engineering discipline will capture AI coding gains sooner.
insights.quote: None of this is new. It's good engineering, built for a new reader.
